Justice Bhuyan was delivering the address at the 12th convocation ceremony of the University of Science and Technology Meghalaya (USTM). He went on to set out what happens to a society that stops asking questions. "A society that accepts claims without evidence is susceptible to superstitious beliefs and becomes vulnerable to mis-information. Referring to Article 51A of the Constitution, which makes developing a scientific temper a fundamental duty of every citizen, the judge said one need not be a scientist to develop it. "Scientific temper or temperament is not confined to or developed in laboratories or scientific institutions. All that you need is the capacity to think rationally; what you say or think must be based on reason," he said, adding that its germination has to take place in the university. He drew a direct line between science and law. "Science is the art of reasoning, so also is law. Science is evidence based, so also is law," he said. The Constitution, he added, has "transposed a deeply feudal society practising graded inequality into a modern forward looking society." items.title: Courting Controversy: Privacy Law, Press Blind Spot
items.summary: In 1972, five men were caught breaking into the offices of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate complex in Washington, DC. What looked like a petty burglary to most, was not considered to be so by two reporters at The Washington Post, Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein. Over the next two years, through late-night phone calls, doorstepping reluctant officials and clandestine meetings, they traced the break-in back to President Richard Nixon’s re-election campaign and, eventually, to the White House itself. Their reporting helped unravel the scandal that forced Nixon to resign in August 1974. Their account of it was made into a film called All the President’s Men , which took its title from Nixon’s aides whose names, money trails and private dealings were painstakingly exposed by the reporters. Now imagine Woodward and Bernstein, before writing a single word, sending a polite note to each of Nixon’s men seeking consent to process their personal data. Imagine, too, the presses grinding to a halt the moment one of them withdrew that consent and demanded that his data be erased. The story, one suspects, would have ended somewhere around chapter one, and Nixon might well have served out his term. That, in essence, is the scenario India’s legacy media has placed before the Supreme Court. On 27 October 2026, the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition by the Digital News Publishers Association (“ DNPA ”) challenging provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (“ DPDP Act ”) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025. DNPA’s 21 members include established media houses and newspapers such as The Indian Express , The Hindu , the Times group, HT Digital, NDTV and Network18. items.title: Karnataka’s voter purge mapped: Bengaluru, women, and young voters bear the brunt
items.summary: For every male voter struck off Karnataka’s electoral rolls during the recently concluded Special Intensive Revision (SIR), two female voters were deleted. No clear pattern in voter deletions in relation to seats held by BJP or Congress could be determined from the draft rolls. These are among the major findings of an analysis of the draft rolls of Karnataka’s SIR by the Sabar Institute. The Sabar Institute analysed the SIR’s deletions against the 2023 and 2018 assembly elections results, the Census 2011, and official district income figures, in its recently released preliminary report. The SIR began in Karnataka on June 20 and the final rolls were published on October 27. In the draft electoral rolls published, one in five people, or 20% of the 2023 electorate, were taken off the rolls for various reasons. The final electoral rolls published on October 27 had 4,55,00,011 names against 5,54,32,314 names in the earlier roll, a decrease of 99,32,303 voters. Sabar Institute’s analysis found that the bulk of deletions, i.e., 85% were due to voters having been marked permanently shifted, untraceable, enrolled elsewhere, or having refused enumeration forms. Over half of these people were under the age of 45. Political parties and SIR It was found that 23% of living voters in BJP-held seats in the state were struck off the rolls compared to 15% in seats held by the Congress. While the gap may look significant, it is almost entirely concentrated in Bengaluru. The BJP holds 16 of the 28 assembly seats in Bengaluru Urban district, and 66 assembly seats in total across the state. The Congress holds 12 seats in Bengaluru and a total of 135 across the state. Karnataka has 224 assembly constituencies. When deletions outside Bengaluru were analysed, Sabar Institute found that the numbers were equal — about 11% of living voters were struck off the rolls in both BJP and Congress held seats. Notably, in 145 of the state’s 224 assembly constituencies – two-third of all seats – the number of living voters removed was higher than the winning margin in the 2023 assembly elections. Vulnerable social groups While a significant gender-based difference was not noticed in the total number of deletions, women’s vulnerability to deletions became visible once the votes deleted due to death were excluded. items.title: COP17 adopts Yerevan Pathway as countries struggle to meet global biodiversity targets
items.summary: The 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17) concluded in Yerevan, Armenia, on October 31, with countries adopting a new roadmap to accelerate global action on biodiversity. The conference's central challenge, however, remains unresolved, as countries have fallen behind on their commitments to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030, with only four years left to meet the targets. The two-week conference adopted nearly 50 decisions, including the Yerevan Pathway, a negotiated response to the first global review of collective progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF). The framework, adopted in 2022, set out 23 targets to be achieved by 2030, including conserving 30% of the world's land and seas, restoring degraded ecosystems, and mobilising resources for biodiversity protection. The first global review of KMGBF, informed by the “State of Biodiversity Action” report released ahead of the conference, found that collective efforts are insufficient to achieve KMGBF’s targets within the stipulated timeframe. The Yerevan Pathway was formulated amid growing concerns over the gap between international commitments and action on the ground. The Pathway identifies priorities for accelerating implementation of KMGBF until 2030. These include reforming subsidies and incentives that harm biodiversity, aligning national budgets and economic decisions with conservation objectives, increasing financial and technical support to developing countries, and strengthening monitoring, reporting, and review mechanisms. "The next four years must bring acceleration and alignment with what we agreed when we adopted the KMGBF," said Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity. "We know what needs to change. We cannot protect nature while continuing to finance its destruction. Resources must reach the countries and communities that need them. Biodiversity must become part of everyday economic decisions. Ultimately, the test is not what governments agreed in Yerevan, but what they change when they return home," she said.
